item.title: US strikes Iranian island ahead of midterm elections
item.description:
Image source, ReutersImage caption,
Donald Trump has been facing falling polling numbers and pressure from within his party to end the warBySareen Habeshian and David GrittenPublished3 November 2026, 03:39 GMTUpdated 1 minute ago
The US has carried out strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, US officials have told CBS, the BBC's US partner.
The officials described the strikes as limited and defensive, and said they were in response to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) firing on a US aircraft.
Iranian state news agency Irna reported explosions on Qeshm on Monday. The IRGC did not comment but said its forces had shot down two US MQM-170 drones south of the island and a US MQ-9 drone east of the Strait of Hormuz.
The US military has not commented on the strikes, which came as mediators stepped up their efforts to prevent a return to all-out war after the US midterm elections on Tuesday.
Trump has been facing falling polling numbers and pressure from within his Republican Party to end the war, which began when the US and Israel attacked Iran in February.
Earlier on Monday, the president told reporters that he was in "no rush" to ramp up strikes on Iran.
"One way or the other, we will do something, but there is no rush. We crippled them financially," he told news outlet Axios. "They have no money, no gasoline and their people are getting very tired of it."
He also said the US "might need to go after Pickaxe [Mountain]", an underground site linked to Iran's nuclear programme, in an interview with Fox News on the eve of the midterms.
This was "not a big deal" and could be done in "one hour", Trump added.
There has been mounting speculation in the last few days that the US may resume significant strikes in Iran again after the midterms. But asked by a reporter on Monday if that was the case, Trump said "no".

item.title: Supreme Court rejects Trump's request to stop California counting disputed votes
item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesBySareen HabeshianReporting fromLos AngelesPublished8 hours ago
The US Supreme Court has rejected a last-minute request by the Trump administration asking it to intervene in California's midterm election vote count.
The justice department wanted 20,000 ballots to be set aside that it alleged may have been issued to non-US citizens in the state.
Two lower courts had already rejected the request. State election officials had questioned the federal government's claims - saying the process used to identify alleged non-citizens was inaccurate.
The Monday ruling comes on the eve of the midterms, which will determine which political party controls the US Congress for the last two years of President Donald Trump's second term.
The Supreme Court announced its decision in a one-line order, saying it was denying the justice department's request for an injunction.
"The application for injunction pending appeal presented to Justice Kagan and by her referred to the Court is denied," it reads.
Its means rulings made in lower courts will stand and essentially ends the Trump administration's bid to disqualify the ballots.
California is the most populous state in America with some 23 million people on its voting register. As of Sunday night, more than six million mail-in ballots had already been received, according to the California secretary of state's office.
What are the US midterms? A simple guide
Published1 hour ago
The justice department sent letters to the California secretary of state and Los Angeles County Registrar last month, demanding they set aside the ballots of 20,000 registered voters whom the Trump administration "believe" are "likely" non-citizens, according to court documents.

item.title: Russian bombing kills 29 people at Ukraine aid centre, Kyiv says
item.description:
To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.
This video can not be playedFigure caption,
Video shows smoke rising from Komyshuvakha blast craterByJaroslav LukivPublished2 November 2026Updated 4 hours ago
At least 29 people were killed after Russian bombs hit an aid distribution centre, in an attack that Ukraine's leader has called "utterly horrific".
Another 10 people were injured and 48 were reported missing after at least nine 3,000kg aerial bombs hit the village of Komyshuvakha in the southern Zaporizhzhia region, regional head Mykhailo Semikin said.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said that after the first strike on the local school "used for humanitarian needs", there was a second attack on the place where people were sheltering.
He posted a video showing a huge crater left after Monday's attack, and rescuer teams searching through the rubble.
The Russian military has not publicly commented.
Image source, DSNS / ZaporizhzhiaImage caption,
There are fears that the death toll will rise further as a number of people are still under the rubble
On Tuesday, regional head Mykhailo Semikin said the death toll had risen to 29 people and that search and rescue operations were ongoing.
"The scale of the tragedy is horrific," he wrote on Telegram.
Zelensky initially put the death toll at 18, but Ukraine's state emergencies service DSNS later said 24 people, including two rescuers and four police officers, were confirmed to have been killed.
In his video address late on Monday, Zelensky said 26 people were now known to have died.
He earlier said that "the Russians could not have been unaware that the local residents who remained in Komyshuvakha received humanitarian aid there every week" on Monday.
"This is yet another proof that Russia does not want any de-escalation."

item.title: Tenerife striker De Miguel dies after on-field collision
item.description:
Image source, AlamyImage caption,
Jesus de Miguel joined Tenerife in 2025 on a three-year dealBySean KearnsBBC Sport senior journalistPublished2 November 2026Updated 2 hours ago
Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel has died after the 30-year-old suffered a serious injury during a Spanish second-division match.
The forward suffered head and chest injuries during a match against FC Andorra on Monday in a heavy collision with goalkeeper Jesus Owono, who was sent off for his challenge.
De Miguel's condition was described as 'stable but serious' on Monday but his health deteriorated on Tuesday morning, with the Spaniard dying at 07:00 GMT (08:00 local time).
"Heartbroken, with a lump in our throats and unable to believe this is true, CD Tenerife announces the tragic death of Jesus de Miguel Alameda," a club statement said.
"There are no words of comfort; there is absolutely nothing that can lessen this overwhelming sadness. We stand with his grieving family, with his loved ones, with all of Tenerife who mourn this cruel loss today."
'There are no words'
Tenerife and Andorra were drawing 2-2 seven minutes into stoppage time when the incident occurred.
Owono ran towards the centre circle to clear a long ball when his knee appeared to collide with De Miguel.
The striker lay motionless on the pitch as medical staff treated him before he was taken by ambulance from Tenerife's Estadio Heliodoro Rodriguez Lopez to hospital.
Players from both teams were visibly distressed by the incident, with a number of De Miguel's team-mates in tears.
The referee showed Owono a straight red card before abandoning the match.
Spanish media, including Marca, reported De Miguel suffered a cardiac arrest in the ambulance and was resuscitated by paramedics on the way to hospital.
Andorra, Tenerife's opponents on Monday, said: "With broken hearts and devastated, we want to send our most sincere condolences to the family of Jesus de Miguel, to all ...

item.title: Jet may have broken apart before Florida crash, officials say, as family named among victims
item.description:
To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.
This video can not be playedFigure caption,
Dashcam footage captures Florida private jet crashByNardine Saad, Kathryn Armstrong and Rachel FlynnPublished2 November 2026Updated 1 hour ago
Investigators believe parts of a private jet which crashed in Florida and killed all nine on board may have broken off in the air.
The Learjet 60 was bound for the Bahamas from Austin, Texas when it nosedived into a multi-lane highway and exploded on impact.
A tech entrepreneur and his young family, as well as the 20-year-old copilot, were among those who died on Sunday.
The US National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said weather conditions would be a major focus of the investigation, but that it was struggling to access the wreckage due to a huge crater on the road which was formed by the jet in Palm Beach.
The plane crashed on Military Trail, a six-lane road that features businesses and restaurants, at around 12:50 local time.
"The biggest obstacle that we're going to have is recovering the major wreckage from the impacted crater on the roadway," lead investigator Tim Monville said at a news conference on Monday.
The NTSB said the crater, near the entrance to a mobile home park, was partially filled with water because of severe storms. Heavy rainfall and thunderstorms had been reported in the area at the time of the crash.
Debris was scattered across sports fields, businesses and homes in the area.
"We do have some evidence that there was some breakup of the aircraft before impact," the NTSB's Tom Chapman said.
"We may find parts of the aircraft some distance away from the actual impact site."
Officials are also trying to find out whether a cockpit voice recorder was on board at the time of the crash and if it can be recovered.
Flight analysis indicates that the jet was plummeting hundreds of feet per second before crashing.

item.title: Asian Cup postponed in wake of attacks on Saudi Arabia
item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption,
Aston Villa will have goalkeeper Zion Suzuki more available this season because of the rescheduling of the Asian CupByMandeep SangheraBBC Sport journalistPublished4 hours ago
The 2027 Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia has been postponed because of a series of deadly attacks on the host country.
The 24-team tournament was scheduled to take place from 7 January to 5 February but has been rescheduled to run from 23 December, 2027 to 21 January, 2028.
In October, a missile attack by Yemen's Houthi movement on Riyadh's airport killed 13 people and wounded more than 300.
A statement from the the Asian Football Confederation (AFC), external said the decision to reschedule had been taken "in light of the current exceptional circumstances arising from developments in the region, including substantial logistical complexities and travel disruptions".
It added: "The new dates of the tournament will be presented to Fifa for approval."
A number of events in Saudi Arabia have been cancelled recently, including the Six Kings Slam tennis exhibition event, which was scheduled to be in Riyadh.
The Asian Tour has also indefinitely postponed it's season-ending golf tournament, which was scheduled to take place from 18-21 November.
This is the second successive Asian Cup to be postponed after the 2023 tournament was moved to 2024 and to Qatar from China because of the Covid pandemic.
Saudi minister vows 'serious response' to Houthi attacks on airports
Published13 October
The decision to postpone the 2027 Asian Cup means a number of Premier League players will not have to miss part of the current season.
Some of the players that would have been expected to be called up were Japan's Zion Suzuki of Aston Villa, Wataru Endo, who plays for Liverpool, and Daizen Maeda of Ipswich Town.

item.title: Thousands of European troops to rehearse Ukraine deployment in event of peace
item.description:
Image source, PA MediaImage caption,
A British paratrooper takes part in a previous Nato training exercise less than 50km (31 miles) from the Russian border in FinlandByJonathan Beale Defence correspondentPublished3 November 2026, 00:07 GMT
Britain and France are to lead a military exercise to test a multinational force's ability to deploy to Ukraine, if there is a peace deal.
Nearly 3,000 military personnel from 12 European nations will take part in the rehearsal in neighbouring Poland this month.
Plans for a reassurance force for Ukraine were set out last year as one of the long-term security guarantees being proposed by European nations.
But there are still more questions than answers as to how such a military force might work in practice. Western officials stress that any force sent to Ukraine would not take part in offensive operations or be involved in peacekeeping or ceasefire monitoring missions.
Nor would they be operating under the command of Nato or on the front line.
Officials say their presence would be to provide reassurance to Ukraine and to help rebuild its armed forces.
The US has been involved in discussions, but is not contributing to the mission.
Russia has already voiced opposition to foreign troops being stationed in Ukraine and, last year, President Vladimir Putin said they would be "legitimate targets".
Western officials have declined to spell out the rules of engagement if any international troops were to be attacked in Ukraine. Though they say the force would be able to defend itself.
UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the exercise showed Britain, France and their allies were stepping up preparation for the day when peace came to Ukraine.
He said: "This is not a hypothetical plan, it's a real force, ready to help Ukraine once the fighting stops."
Lt Gen Tom Bateman, the UK commander of the Multi National Force – Ukraine (MNF-U), said the exercise represented an important step in translating political commitmen...

item.description:
To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.
This video can not be playedFigure caption,
'All this food is now useless': Piles of rubbish after shop freezers hit by cyber-attackByJames GregoryPublished2 November 2026
Dozens of supermarkets across seven European countries have been hit by a cyber-attack affecting their refrigerators and freezers.
Around 40 Delhaize supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected, while a smaller number of shops were hit in Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.
Sabcobel, a Belgian company that manufactures some of the affected refrigerators, said the units' evaporators were switched to defrost mode, causing them to warm up, in what is believed to be the same method used in last month's incident that hit hundreds of French supermarkets.
Millions of euros worth of food had to be thrown away in October, local media reported at the time.
Image source, TT NEWS AGENCY / AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption,
Freezers have had to be emptied at several ICA grocery stores in Sweden after the cyber-attack
Stephan Moelans, the CEO of Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize's systems, on Monday told the Belga news agency that the incident was a cyber-attack and that the company had been "working all night and morning to disconnect the affected units from the network".
He said since the French attack in early October, the company had been working to "protect our customers fridges against this vulnerability" but that the units needed physical modifications, not just software updates.
Most supermarkets across Europe are linked to the internet, and maintenance and troubleshooting can be done remotely.
"The simplest solution is to manage the fridges over a secure internet connection. Most of our customers switched to that after the attack in France," Moelans added.
The temperature of freezers in several shops across Europe reportedly rose to as high as 50C (122F).

item.title: Trump to remove Rwanda and South Africa from US trade deal
item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption,
Last year, Trump accused South Africa of white genocide in a meeting with President Cyril Ramaphosa at the White HouseByAllan OlingoPublished2 November 2026Updated 1 hour ago
US President Donald Trump has notified Congress of his intention to remove South Africa and Rwanda from a preferential trade programme, from 1 January 2027.
The African Growth and Opportunity Act (Agoa) allows eligible African countries to export thousands of products to the US duty-free.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a statement that an annual review had found that both countries were engaging in practices inconsistent with the programme's eligibility requirements.
He added that the Trump administration had additionally notified the two countries of the decision.
The Trump administration cited barriers to US trade and investment, as well as concerns over national security and foreign policy interests in the region.
For South Africa, the US pointed to corruption.
In a letter to South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, Trump said Pretoria's actions on international security and its relations and cooperation with governments of concern to Washington risked undermining US national security and foreign policy interests.
He also accused South Africa of maintaining significant barriers to American trade and investment, including restrictions affecting agricultural market access, regulatory requirements, investment protections and intellectual property.
"The Trump administration is working to ensure our African partners take the necessary steps to meet the eligibility criteria," Greer said.
South Africa's Trade Minister Parks Tau described the decision as "unfortunate", saying Washington was raising new issues that had not featured in trade negotiations between the two countries, which began in 2025.
"We will continue to accelerate the diversification of South Africa's export markets to protect jobs," Tau said. ...

item.title: Fighting returns to Kherson region after longest Ukraine war ceasefire
item.description:
Image source, ReutersImage caption,
Hundreds of Oleshky evacuees arrived back in Ukraine on Saturday after years trapped on the frontlineByLaura Gozzi and Vitaly Shevchenko, Chief analyst, BBC MonitoringPublished2 November 2026
Fighting has resumed in Ukraine's Kherson after a six-day truce brought quiet to the front-line region for the first time in years.
The ceasefire - the longest since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022 - allowed hundreds of people trapped in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky and its surroundings to be evacuated.
On Monday morning, local authorities confirmed that strikes had resumed, saying Moscow had hit a medical facility in Kherson city centre. They also said a 62-year-old woman and a 73-year-old man were injured when a Russian drone attacked the car they were travelling in.
Ukraine also accused Russian forces of using the humanitarian ceasefire to strengthen their military positions, rotate units and deliver ammunition.
"The enemy used the humanitarian pause to set up their positions," said Ukraine's General Staff, adding they had recorded rotation of Russian units, expansion of anti-drone equipment on the roads, and delivery of ammunition.
The Kremlin appeared to corroborate this when spokesman Dmitry Peskov said it was "reasonable to assume that the Ukrainian army also used this period for the necessary regrouping".
"It is a completely standard practice in such situations," he added.
The ceasefire had been brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump. Both Kyiv and Moscow thanked her repeatedly, though no details of her involvement were shared.
An unusual show of cooperation came from Russia's human rights ombudsman Yana Lantratova and her Ukrainian counterpart Dmytro Lubinets. The pair oversaw the ceasefire, travelled into Oleshky and were filmed speaking to residents together.
